title: 3% growth or 2%: does it matter?
hook: Two countries start equal. One grows a point faster. How far apart in a lifetime?

knows: that growth compounds year on year
what a percentage growth rate is
doesNotKnow: that a one-point difference in growth rate changes income a lot over generations

misconception: 3% growth and 2% growth are nearly the same.
objective: The learner can explain that the growth gap compounds too, so after 70 years a country growing 3% a year is about twice as rich as one growing 2% (7.92 vs 4.00).

claims.text: Growing 3% a year for 70 years multiplies income by 7.92; growing 2% multiplies it by 4.00.
After 70 years the 3% country is 1.98 times as rich as the 2% country (about double).
The gap compounds: 1.03 ÷ 1.02 ≈ 1.0098 a year, and 1.0098^70 ≈ 1.98.
With a gap of 0.5 points (2.5% vs 2%) the ratio after 70 years is 1.41; with 2 points (4% vs 2%) it is 3.89.
claims.source: 1.025^70 / 1.02^70 = 1.408; 1.04^70 / 1.02^70 = 3.893. Shown in the reveal only for gaps the learner viewed at year 70.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: steady growth every year, invented rates, no shocks; not any country's record and not a forecast.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: steady growth, invented rates'.

recall.question: Country A grows 1 percentage point a year faster than country B, steadily. Over a long lifetime, the gap between them…
options: compounds, so A can end up about twice as rich
recall.why: Each year's growth builds on the last, so the ratio grows by about 1% a year, compounding to roughly double over 70 years.
